abs_metadata.title: LeapQuant: Efficient Linear Attention with Accurate Recurrent State Quantization
abs_metadata.affiliations_from_paper: UC Berkeley, University of Washington, MIT, Perplexity AI, NVIDIA (Yi Pan and Haocheng Xi equal contribution)
abs_metadata.license: CC BY 4.0 (stated on the HTML version)

abstract_claims.hardware: NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090

abs_metadata.abstract_quote_e2e: it achieves average speedups of 2.05--3.70$\times$ at the kernel level and 1.47$\times$ for end-to-end inference on NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090 GPUs.
abs_metadata.discrepancy: The abs-page abstract says 1.47x; the v2 PDF (p.1 abstract, p.2 intro) and v2 HTML say 1.57x. 1.47x is the v1 value (mean of v1 Figure 9's 18 cells = 1.4672); 1.57x is the mean of v2 Figure 9's 24 cells (1.5667).

project_page.summary: Restates the v2 claims (1.57x, not the abs-page 1.47x). Its accuracy table equals paper Table 1 exactly; its kernel, decode and end-to-end images show the same labels as paper Figures 7, 8 and 9. No sampling settings, software versions or H100 mention on the page.

text_source_notes: Full text from arxiv.org/html/2609.38166v2 (parsed with a python3 stdlib HTML parser). Cross-checked against the v2 PDF text extracted with macOS PDFKit (osascript -l JavaScript); all table numbers match the PDF. Figure values come from the SVG figure files served with the HTML version (glyph data-text attributes + exact bar/line geometry mapped through axis ticks) and were visually verified on PDFKit renders of PDF pages 2, 4, 8, 9, 16. Page numbers refer to the PDF.

global_settings_from_paper.implementation: LeapQuant implemented in vLLM; linear-attention decode kernels in TileLang; compensator tokens fitted with power iteration at each window boundary; other components (e.g. MoE layers) stay in baseline precision
global_settings_from_paper.default_config: we use a window of p = 16 tokens, r = 4 FP16 Compensator Tokens (r = 6 at 6 and 4 bits), and FP32 smoothing scales
global_settings_from_paper.efficiency_baseline: FP32-state implementation of vLLM with CUDA graphs enabled (decode and end-to-end); FP32 kernel in FLA (kernel)
global_settings_from_paper.gpus: NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, RTX 5090 (no H100/Hopper anywhere in v2)
global_settings_from_paper.software_versions: none stated (vLLM, SGLang, FLA, TileLang, CUDA, PyTorch versions absent)
global_settings_from_paper.quality_eval: accuracy averaged over three random seeds; USACO and OJBench single runs; sampling per Table 5; same prompts/sample set across methods; concurrency capped so no request is preempted

cells.quote: average speedups of 2.05--3.70$\times$ at the kernel level and 1.47$\times$ for end-to-end inference on NVIDIA B200, RTX PRO 6000, and RTX 5090 GPUs
cells.notes: Stale v1 value: the v1 abstract (abs/2609.38166v1 and html/2609.38166v1) says 1.47x; v1 Figure 9 had only 18 cells (Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, Kimi-Linear-48B-A3B x {B200, RTX PRO 6000} x {GSM, MMLU, GPQA}), identical to the corresponding v2 cells, mean 1.4672 -> 1.47. v2 added GLM-5.3-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on B200 (6 cells), mean of 24 -> 1.57, but the v2 abs-page abstract was not updated. (The 9 RTX PRO 6000 cells alone also average 1.4689.)

cells.state_precision: BF16
cells.sample_counts: averaged over three seeds
cells.quote: Naive FP8/INT8 state quantization collapses on Qwen3.5-9B, and even BF16 loses 11.5 points on average, while LeapQuant matches FP32 at 8 and 6 bits
cells.notes: = Avg column 84.0 - 72.5 (unrounded 84.050 - 72.542 = 11.51). The BF16 numbers equal paper Table 1 BF16 row, i.e. per-step BF16.

cells.metric: average accuracy gap of LeapQuant 4-bit vs FP32 over 12 pairs
cells.quote: LeapQuant matches FP32 at 8 and 6 bits and stays within 3.4 points at 4 bits.
cells.notes: 84.0 - 80.6 on the Avg column. Per-task 4-bit gaps are larger on GLM-5.3-Flash (BeyondAIME 80.7 -> 69.0 = 11.7 points; LCB 85.2 -> 75.3 = 9.9).

cells.metric: which BF16 baseline variant the accuracy table uses
cells.reported_value: per-step BF16 (state re-stored in BF16 after every decode step); not windowed
cells.state_precision: BF16
cells.quote: per-step quantization leads to poor accuracy even at 16 bits: storing the Qwen3.5-9B state in BF16 lowers its AIME score from 87.9% to 72.1%
cells.notes: Quote from paper Sec. 4.2 (p.7-8). The project page only labels the row "BF16". Supporting evidence: paper Table 2 lists "BF16 per-step" = AIME 72.1, LCB 49.6 (identical to the BF16 row of Table 1/page) and a separate "+ Per-window" BF16 row = 87.8 / 62.9 (ablation only, Qwen3.5-9B). Sec. 4.1: baselines include "the FP32 and BF16 states, the default and optional formats in vLLM and SGLang"; App. E: "all baselines re-quantize the state at every decode step."
